LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS
There are, according to latest published figures, 613,209 Girl Guides in the world.
The Colony had a clean bill of health on Thursday, no case of notifiable disease being reported.
Annual subscriptions to the local Boy Scout Association are due on October 1:—(a) minimum for membership $5 and (b) "Silver Wolf" Fund $5.
A picked detachment of 24 from the Scottish Company, H.K.V.D.C., will meet the King's Own Scottish Borders on their arrival in Hong Kong.
Paris, September. 22.—Le Martin reports that Druse attacked three French soundrons north-east of Damascus. The Druse fled leaving ten dead.
In November, Miss Trotter (District Commissioner, East Herts) and Miss Wanklyn (District Commissioner, Cheshunt) are coming to Hong Kong to conduct a four months' training of Girl Guides and Guiders.

Technical Institute classes resume on Monday. Entry forms can be obtained by applicants at the Education Dept. (for attendance at Queen's College) and at the Central British School (for classes in Kowloon).

Nauen, September 16.—A report from Moscow states that a British note has arrived in Moscow on the Algeciras question. The British Foreign Office is of the opinion that the agreement made with the Czariist Government at Algeciras is to be considered invalid as the Soviet Government nullified all treaties made by the Czariist Government.

Peking, September 11.—The Cabinet to-day requested the Foreign and Education Ministries to re-examine the revision suggested by the Ministry of Education. Article 10 of the Sino-Japanese Far Eastern Cultural Enterprises Regulations, namely, that all business matters relating to the Cultural Enterprises shall receive the approval of the majority of both the Chinese and the Japanese Commissioners.
At yesterday's Council meeting, the Attorney-General elaborated on the reasons for the introduction of measures to empower the Governor to appoint such as he thought, as Registrar of Marriages; also for powers with regard to pay and discipline of Volunteers during the annual Camp. The second reading was also passed of the Ordinance to charge the Loan to the Colony on the general revenue and assets of the Colony.

Peking, Sept. 23.—In a manifesto, issued by the Shanghai District Kuomintang Party, and reproduced by the "Minkuppa", this morning, England is described as "the most tyrannical of all the imperialistic nations and the strongest power in the East: 90 per cent. of the Oriental people are under the oppression of Britain," the manifesto states "therefore it we are to carry out our anti-imperialistic activities we should regard England as our principal opponent."

Hankow, September 24.—The first train to bring foreign residents from Chikungshah to Hankow since the retirement of Marshall Wu Pei-fu arrived at six o'clock yesterday evening. According to statements brought down by those who came down the South Valley residents experienced a dreadful time after the capture of the place by the Southern forces, whose exemplary behaviour was illustrated by looting several of the bungalows. It is now stated that the Railway will run a daily train to and from Sintiens from now on.

With the approval of the Shanghai authorities, the Shanghai Rice Guild proposes, as from today, October 1, to take definite steps to regulate the price of rice. The plans have not been made public but it is understood that rice merchants will be asked to hang out signboards showing that they are members of the guild and informing the people that they are selling the grain at reasonable and regulated prices. The public will be asked to deal only with these places and not to go near any shop which cannot prove its affiliation with the guild as such generally turn out to be an agency of the profiteering ring.

The board of management of Milton Mount College has appointed as head mistress Mrs. Dorothy M. Henman, widow of an officer who fell in the war. Mrs. Henman is the daughter of the late Dr. G. H. Bondfield, who did such fine missionary work in China, and niece of Miss Margaret Bondfield, the Labour leader. She has a successful career at Ginton and was head mistress of the Shanghai High School and later of the Cathedral School for Girls, Shanghai.
Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf of Sweden neither smokes nor drinks. That fact has caused interest in this democratic heir to the throne of Sweden all the way around the world on his present tour. He was the subject of countless interviews and newspaper comment in America last summer and nearly all of them queried him on this subject. He is similar to the Prince Regent of Japan in this regard. Japan's present Regent also is a total abstainer and does not smoke. Sweden's Crown Prince told American news writers he hadn't smoked nor taller alcoholic beverages for more than 15 years.

London, Sept. 13.—The “Morning Post” says that Sir Prodyat Tagore has commissioned the well-known artist, Mr. Jacob Hood, to paint the portrait of Lord Lytton for the Victoria Hall, Caicutta. After the completion of the work the artist will proceed to India to paint the portraits of Sir Prodyat Tagore and his wife and son and the Maharajah of Burdwan.
Reminder: Farewell dinner of El Gloria Lodge, No. 5872, R.A.O.B., in the Royal Naval theatre, at 8 p.m. to-morrow.
SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
Paris, September 13.—M. Marin presided at the solemn inaugural ceremonies in Sarrebourg of the cemetery for French nationals who died while prisoners of Germany during the World War.

Näuen, September 9.—According to a dispatch from Moscow, the Chinese Chamber of Commerce at Harbin has demanded that Russia turn over to China 66 villages situated on the left side of the Amur river, which were occupied during the Boxer Revolt. Russia is said flatly to have refused the demands.

Madras, Sept. 12.—Viscountess Goschen, who arrived in Bombay on the s.s. "Rajputana" after four months' stay in England, returned to Madras this morning, accompanied by Miss Portal and two A.D.C.'s. His Excellency the Governor and members of the Cabinet gave her a cordial welcome at the station.

Shanghai, September 16.—General Liu Tao-lung, commander of the Hankow-Hanyang Defence Forces, yesterday said a visit to the Japanese Consulates at Hankow and formally apologised for the recent firing incident wherein the Japanese warship "Katada" was attacked by Chinese troops.

San Diego, California, September 16.—Vico Consul Fukuoka, a Japanese Vice-Consul of Los Angeles, has arrived here to investigate the machine-gunning of the Japanese schooner "Iwate" by the Mexican fisheries patrol steamer "Tecate" recently. It is reported that the Japanese Government will lodge a protest against the capture and firing happened outside Mexican or American territorial waters.
A concert is to be given in the Chinese Y.M.C.A. to-morrow at 8 p.m. by the 20th Hong Kong Troop of Boy Scouts on the first anniversary of their formation.

Peking, Sept. 18.—According to a recent census made by the Ministry of Interior, the statistics for foreigners in Peking according to occupations read as follows: Students, 683; those engaged in commerce and industry, 566; missionaries, 121; teachers 50; doctors, 6; prostitutes, 59; those engaged in communication, 37; in mining and fishing, 11; in agriculture and forestry, 5; and lawyers, 2.
Do not forget the opening show by Dick Norton's Globetrotters at the "Star" Theatre, Kowloon, at 9.15 p.m. to-morrow.

Moścow, September 16.—The Commintern (Headquarters of the Third Internationale) issued a manifesto to-day, strongly expressing its opposition to any reinforcement of forces in China on the part of the Powers, especially of Britain. Meanwhile, in view of the recent development of the situation in China, various anti-foreign agitations are going on in Russia under the watchword of "Non-interference with Chinese internal politics." Anti-British agitation is particularly active.
The many friends in Hong Kong of Mr. Walter Sinclair will be interested to know that he has been re-appointed Director of the Hait House Theatre, Toronto, for the season 1926-27.

The following have been granted commissions in the Hong Kong Volunteer Defence Corps, C.S.M., J. E. Hancock (Armoured Company), Sgt. N. L. H. Rallton (Artillery Co.) and Sapper M. G. Noll (Engineer Co.)

Mr. W. H. Edmonds of the Water Works, who, is a musketry expert, has received the substantive appointment of Regimental Sergeant Major in the Defence Corps, having held "acting" rank for some time. He goes on leave till July 31 next year.

The programme of the Feast of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary at Nosary Church, Kowloon, on Sunday is as follows:—First Mass, 8.30 a.m.; Second Mass, 7.30 a.m.; Third Mass, 8.30 a.m.; Solemn Pontifical Mass, 9.30 a.m. Evening Service is at 4:30 p.m.

The late Mr. Andrew Adam Bolton, an engineer at the Talkood Dock who died at sea whilst on a homeward voyage by the s.s. "Montclare" on June 16 of this year, left property in Hong Kong, amounting to $10,200. He left everything to his widow, Mrs. Mary Isabella Bolton.

"The Feast of the Little Flower," St. Theresa of the Child of Jesus, — who was canonised last year— was solemnly celebrated at the Roman Catholic Cathedral yesterday. The celebration of the feast consisted of a solemn High Mass sung at 7:30 a.m., and a solemn Holy Hour with sermon and Benediction from 5:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Special music under the direction of the Rev. Father A. Riganti was sung in the morning as in the afternoon service.

Hong Kong is shortly to have a distinguished visitor in the person of Dr. John Allison, M.A., LL.D., J.R.S.E., who recently retired from the Headmastership of George Watson's College, Edinburgh. He is at present on a world tour of Watsonian Clubs and is due here on November 22. Old Watsonians who wish to join in extending hospitality to Dr. Allison are asked to communicate with Mr. John Fleming, of Messrs. Lowe, Bingham and Matthews.
Paris, Sept. 18.—According to "Le Petit Parisien," Krassin is to proceed to London during the week end, and will become the Soviet Charge d'Affaires.
London, September 22.—Lord d'Abernon is leaving the Berlin post on October 6. He will give a banquet before leaving at which President Hindenberg will be the guest of honour.

Berlin, Sept. 18.—Dr. Shurman, American Ambassador to Berlin, is going to Washington via Cherbourg to participate in a financial conference with President Coolidge and the British and French Ambassadors to the United States. The Paris Press believes that this may foreshadow a revision of the American policy regarding the French war-debts.

Peking, Sept. 20.—Mr. David Fraser, Peking correspondent of the London "Times," who has been home on holiday, returned to Peking to-day. He came by way of Russia and Siberia, making the trip from London to Peking in thirteen days. Mr. W. H. Donald, Director of the Government Bureau of Economic Information, who has been substituting for Mr. Fraser during the latter's absence, will leave Peking for Shanghai to be gone for two weeks.

Hankow, Sept. 24.—While two ladies were getting into ricshas yesterday a long-gowned Chinese of the student type came up and spoke to the coolies. As it happened one of the ladies knew the language and was interested to hear the intruder state that the ricsha pullers had promised at the mass labour meeting held on Wednesday not to have foreign passengers in future. He then requested the two coolies to keep their promise. Needless to say they did so by refusing to take the ladies.

Peking, Sept. 17 — Mr. Miao Po-tao, Associate editor of the Chinese service of this agency, was released at seven o'clock last evening after about nine hours' detention in the headquarters of the Yichun army. He was queried as to the origin of a report which appeared in a recent issue of the Chinese service to the effect that some Yichun troops in Homan ignored the order of General Kou Ying-chiah to co-operate with his troops in the Suppression of Bandibry in that province. In reply Mr. Miao said that the report came from the Homan correspondent of this agency, and offered to produce the original version.
